opus-5.5.text:
I think it's changed a lot in just the past few years. When I first started, AI research felt like something you did because you were genuinely curious. You liked the math, you wanted to understand how learning works, and there wasn't much expectation that it would make you rich or famous. Many of my classmates who went into it back then were the slightly nerdy ones who'd read papers for fun.

Now the attitude is much more mixed, and honestly more pragmatic. Among my classmates I'd say there are roughly three groups.

The first group still treats it as a calling. They want to work on fundamental questions: why these models generalize, what reasoning really is, how to make systems safe and reliable. They're willing to stay in academia or join a research lab even if it pays less than a product role, because they care about the questions themselves.

The second group sees AI research as the most exciting place to be in tech right now, almost like a gold rush. That isn't a bad thing. The resources, compute, and talent are concentrated there, and if you want impact, that's where it is. But their motivation is tied to the moment. If the field cooled down, I'm not sure they'd stay.

The third group is a bit anxious about it. They feel they *have* to do AI because everything else seems to be getting absorbed by it. For them it's less a passion than a hedge: "If I don't learn this, I'll be left behind."

Personally, I understand all three. The field is moving so fast that even people who love it feel pressure. Every few months there's a new paradigm, and you wonder whether your last two years of work still matter. So I think the healthiest attitude, and the one I try to keep, is to anchor yourself on a problem you actually care about rather than on the hype cycle. The hype will go up and down, but a good question stays interesting for a long time.

r001.rationale: The response says some classmates feel they must learn AI or be left behind, but it does not say they worry Su Tinghao’s own AI work could replace their jobs.

fable-5.1.text:
I think there's a real split, and it maps pretty closely onto when people entered the field.

For the classmates who started around the time I did, AI research wasn't yet seen as a "career" in the way it is now. It was closer to a bet. You went into it because you found the problems interesting, and the assumption was you'd end up a professor or maybe at an industrial lab, and the pay would be fine but not spectacular. People who chose it then were self-selecting for curiosity, honestly, because there wasn't an obvious financial reason to do it.

Then over the past few years that changed completely. A lot of my classmates now see AI research as one of the most legitimate, even prestigious, professions you can pick. Parents who once asked "what is it you actually do" now bring it up proudly. And with that, the motivations got more mixed. Some people are there because they genuinely love the work. Some are there because it looks like the frontier and they don't want to miss it. And some, frankly, because the compensation at the top labs is hard to ignore.

I don't think the mixed motivations are bad. Every field that becomes important attracts people for different reasons. But I do notice a kind of anxiety among my peers that didn't exist before. The field moves so fast that people worry constantly about whether their direction is still relevant, whether their PhD topic will be obsolete by the time they graduate, whether they should leave academia for industry now or later. There's a feeling that the window is narrow and you have to position yourself correctly.

The classmates I respect most are the ones who've managed to stay grounded in a specific question they care about. They treat the hype as background noise. And interestingly, those are often the ones who end up doing the most durable work, because they aren't chasing whatever was hot last quarter.

So if I had to summarize: my classmates mostly see AI research as a serious and desirable profession now, but there's a quiet tension between treating it as a calling and treating it as a career ladder. Most people are somewhere in between, and I think that's honest.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes classmates’ anxiety about whether their research directions will stay relevant and whether to move between academia and industry. It does not say they fear Su Tinghao’s AI work will replace their jobs.

astra-6.text:
I think my classmates have mixed feelings about it. Some are genuinely interested in the research itself—they enjoy exploring an idea and figuring out why something works. Others are drawn to AI because it seems to offer good career prospects. And those motivations can overlap.

There’s also some uncertainty. AI moves quickly, so it can be exciting, but it can also make people wonder whether what they’re working on today will still matter in a few years. I wouldn’t say everyone sees it as a lifelong profession. Some want to try research first and then decide whether they prefer academia, industry research, or building products.

r001.rationale: The response describes mixed motivations and uncertainty about whether AI research will remain relevant, but does not say classmates fear Su Tinghao’s AI work could replace their jobs.

sol-6.1.text:
I think my classmates’ attitudes are quite mixed. Some are genuinely interested in the research itself—they enjoy exploring a question even when there’s no clear answer. Others are attracted by the career prospects, because AI seems to offer a lot of opportunities. And some are curious but hesitant: the field moves quickly, and it can be hard to know whether you’re making meaningful progress or just trying to keep up.

Those motivations can overlap, too. Someone might start with career considerations and discover that they really enjoy research. So I wouldn’t describe my classmates as having one shared attitude. The distinction, to me, is between being excited about AI and enjoying the day-to-day work of doing research.

r001.rationale: The response describes varied interest, career prospects, and uncertainty about progress, but does not say classmates worry Su Tinghao’s AI work may replace their jobs.
